paras: The lynching of Smith near Little Rock was the killing of a Black man known only as Smith by a disguised party in Arkansas on or about August 24, 1882. He was accused of attempting to outrage a white woman, and a wire dispatch reporting that he had been shot to death ran in papers across the country within days.

According to the Daily Globe, Smith was accused of attempting on Monday, August 21, to outrage 'a white lady in the vicinity of Little Rock.' The woman was not named in any report, and no paper gave Smith's first name; The Frontier said only that he 'used to live near Little Rock.'

A dispatch dated Little Rock, August 24, stated that 'advices' had been received there that Smith had been lynched by a disguised party, who shot him to death. The Cheyenne Daily Leader's version said he had been 'taken by a disguised party,' but no report said where he was seized or where he was killed. The National Republican placed the lynching near Little Rock and said the 'masked party' riddled his body with bullets. No paper gave the size of the party, the time of day, or whether anyone watched.
No report of an arrest, inquest, grand-jury inquiry or trial connected with the killing appears in the coverage, and no Arkansas paper's account was found.

The dispatch first appeared on August 24 in the Alexandria Gazette, the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and the Washington Evening Star, and a Chicago relay of the same 'Little Rock special' reached the Rock Island Argus that day. On August 25 it ran in New York, Memphis, St. Paul, Washington, Sacramento, Cheyenne and Eureka, and western weeklies carried it through the end of the month. Further printings appeared in the Tombstone Weekly Epitaph and the Arizona Weekly Citizen.

Most papers kept the dispatch's wording that Smith 'attempted' an outrage, but several headlines treated the charge as proven: the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer ran 'A Brute Lynched,' the Evening Star 'An Outrager Lynched,' the Memphis Daily Appeal 'Rapist Shot to Death,' and the Eureka Daily Sentinel 'A Ravisher Shot to Death.' The Tombstone Weekly Epitaph headed the item 'Served Him Right,' while the Sacramento Daily Record-Union used the more cautious 'Reported Lynching.' Only some versions named Smith's race; the New-York Tribune headed its item 'A Negro Lynched in Arkansas.'

As the story was condensed into weekly digests, the alleged attempt became a completed act: the Semi-Weekly Interior Journal wrote that Smith 'assaulted a white lady,' and The Frontier that he 'committed an outrage upon a white lady.'

The original wire said only that Smith was shot to death by a disguised party. The Morning Journal and Courier instead reported that he had been 'hanged by a mob,' and The Frontier said his neighbors 'hung him to a tree and shot him full of holes.' Neither of the later versions named a source beyond the wire, which remained the earliest account.

reader.title: Lynching of Smith near Little Rock
bases: A Little Rock dispatch reported that a disguised party shot Smith to death after he was accused of attempting to outrage a white woman (A3, A12, A19).

Every version says Smith was killed by a 'disguised party,' 'masked party,' 'mob' or his 'neighbors' with no legal process, in answer to an alleged sexual offense against a white woman (A3, A19, A18, A32); no paper gives the party's size, but every term used names a group, and the papers call it a lynching.
All printings trace to one Little Rock dispatch of August 24 (A3, A5, A14), and the later variants with a hanging (A18, A32) cite no separate source; no Arkansas paper or follow-up report was found.

framing.detail: Headlines treated the accusation as fact or approved the killing: 'A Brute Lynched,' 'Rapist Shot to Death,' 'Served Him Right.'
Most papers ran the one-sentence dispatch unchanged, some under neutral heads such as 'Lynched' or 'Reported Lynching.'
